What should a seller know about Kansas City, MO before listing?

Kansas City is Missouri's largest city by both population and area, and it spreads across four counties: Jackson, Clay, Platte and Cass. Whichever county holds your house decides which recorder files the deed and which collector bills the property tax, so check the parcel record before you sign anything.

The Missouri River and the Kansas River meet here. The town of Kansas was incorporated on June 1, 1850, became the City of Kansas in 1853, and took the name Kansas City in 1889. The Census Bureau lists 314.70 square miles of land, so conditions change a lot from a Northland subdivision to a Brookside bungalow to a Crossroads loft.

How large is the Kansas City housing market according to the Census?

Kansas City had an estimated 521,220 residents in mid-2025, up 2.6 percent from a 508,012 base in April 2020. There are 221,979 households and about 55 percent of homes are owner occupied.

  • Middle home value among owners (2020 to 2024): $242,900
  • Median gross rent: $1,238
  • Median household income: $69,166
  • Average commute: 21.7 minutes
  • Language other than English at home: 13.1 percent

Those are citywide middle values. A house in Brookside or the Northland can sit far from them, so ask for a price opinion tied to the specific block and to recent closed sales.

Which neighborhoods, districts and highways matter to Kansas City buyers?

More than 240 neighborhoods make up the city. South of the Country Club Plaza, the Country Club District takes in Sunset Hill and Brookside along Ward Parkway, known for large historic homes. The River Market is the original neighborhood on the Missouri River, and 18th and Vine, Westport and Crossroads are among the districts that attract urban buyers. The Northland is where population has grown fastest.

Kansas City has no single school district. Fifteen districts serve parts of the city, and Kansas City Public Schools covers the inner core. Buyers with children will check which district a street falls in before anything else, so name it in every listing or direct offer conversation.

The highway grid is dense: I-29, I-35, I-49, I-70, I-435, I-470, I-635 and I-670, plus US 24, 40, 50, 56, 69, 71 and 169. I-435 rings the whole city. Easy access to those routes is a selling point for commuters and for anyone who works in the metro's logistics sector.

Which ways of selling a Kansas City house should I compare?

Kansas City owners generally weigh three paths: a traditional listing, a private sale, and a direct sale to a cash buyer. The size of the city means timelines vary widely by area, so base your choice on the house in front of you.

  • Traditional listing: suits a house in good shape in a district buyers search by name, such as the Plaza area or the Northland. Expect showings, an appraisal and a buyer inspection.
  • Private sale: you handle pricing and paperwork, and the Jackson County recorder will not complete forms for you.
  • Cash buyer: fits inherited, vacant or tenant-occupied houses where repairs or registrations are the obstacle. Ask for the offer in writing and compare it with a listing estimate.

Transit can help marketing. The KC Streetcar runs from Union Station to the River Market, Amtrak's Southwest Chief and Missouri River Runner stop in the city, and Kansas City's freeway network gives most addresses quick access to downtown. List those facts only when your street actually benefits from them.

What drives jobs and housing demand in Kansas City?

Federal offices are a large part of the metro economy. The IRS runs a service center here with about 2,700 full-time employees, growing to 4,000 in tax season, and the Kansas City Federal Reserve Bank opened a new building near Union Station in 2008. Hallmark Cards is headquartered at Crown Center, and H&R Block's world headquarters is a 20-story glass oval tower.

The University of Missouri-Kansas City, Rockhurst University, Park University and Metropolitan Community College add student and staff renters. Summer highs average around 90 in July, winters swing cold, and the city sits in plant hardiness zones 5b and 6a, so roofs, HVAC and gutters get tested in both seasons.

What city registrations apply to Kansas City homes that are rented or empty?

Kansas City runs three programs that sellers of non-owner-occupied property run into. Each has its own office and calendar, so confirm status before a buyer's title work begins.

City of Kansas City programs for rented or vacant homes (source: kcmo.gov)
ProgramWhat it requires
Healthy Homes Rental Inspection ProgramAll rental owners register under Ordinance 180248; proof of ownership such as a Closing Disclosure, a photo ID and the fee are required; fees changed January 1, 2026; office at 2400 Troost Ave., Suite 3600, 816-513-6464
Vacant Property RegistrationNon-owner-occupied vacant or foreclosed units register online each year between December 1 and January 31; no fee when on time; $50 late penalty; newly vacant property within 90 days, foreclosed property within 14 days
Short-Term Rental registrationAnnual registration through CompassKC; not transferable to a new owner; fines of $200 to $1,000 for operating without one

One detail helps sellers: the vacant property definition excludes a property that a licensed real estate professional is currently marketing, as long as water service has not been shut off. The next vacant property window opens December 1, 2026.

What if the city has cited my Kansas City house for a code violation?

The Property Maintenance Appeals Board hears appeals of Notice and Order citations under Chapter 56 and nuisance orders. An appeal must be filed within 10 calendar days from the date printed on the notice and comes with a non-refundable $50 fee. Hearings are on the second Thursday of each month at 9:30 a.m. at City Hall, 414 E. 12th St., on the eighth floor.

Short-term rental rules matter at sale time too. Non-resident short-term rentals are barred in residentially zoned areas, and a registration cannot be passed to the next owner. If your house was a rental on Airbnb or VRBO, tell buyers that the new owner must start a fresh application.

How do I record the deed in Jackson County and what does it cost?

For a Kansas City address in Jackson County, deeds are recorded by the Recorder of Deeds at the Jackson County Courthouse, 415 E 12th Street, Room 104, phone 816-881-3191. A second office is in the Historic Truman Courthouse in Independence. Parcels in the Clay, Platte or Cass County portions of the city are recorded by those counties instead.

The county posts a standard charge of $23 for page one, then $3 per added page, and notes that documents received on or after August 28, 2026 fall under the new fee schedule. Card payments at the counter carry a 2.75 percent processing fee. The office reviews and indexes documents but cannot fill in forms for you, and photocopies are not accepted. RSMo 442.380 calls for recording with the recorder of the county where the land is.

More questions about Kansas City, MO

Which county do I deal with if I sell a Kansas City house?

The county where the parcel lies. Kansas City reaches into Jackson, Clay, Platte and Cass counties, and each has its own recorder.

Do I have to register an empty Kansas City house?

Yes if it is a vacant or foreclosed unit the owner does not occupy. Register online between December 1 and January 31, with a $50 late penalty after that. A property that a licensed real estate professional is marketing, with the water still on, does not count as vacant.

Can a buyer take over my short-term rental registration?

No. Kansas City registrations are not transferable. The new owner has to apply on their own through CompassKC.

What is the deadline to appeal a Kansas City code violation?

Ten calendar days from the date on the notice. The filing fee is $50 and hearings are held monthly on the second Thursday.

What does the Healthy Homes program ask of rental owners?

Every rental owner must register under Ordinance 180248 with a photo ID, a federal tax ID letter when applicable, the fee, and proof of ownership such as a Closing Disclosure or recorded deed. New fees took effect January 1, 2026. Call 816-513-6464 for current amounts.

Which selling route fits a house in St. Louis, MO?

Three routes exist for a St. Louis homeowner: hire a broker, go it alone, or hand the keys to an investor who pays cash for the property in its present condition. All three lead to the same city checkpoint, a Housing Conservation inspection that produces a Certificate of Inspection before the next household moves in.

Time is the real trade. Putting a house on the market invites the widest audience, yet you will clean, stage and sit through showings while a buyer's lender works through underwriting. An investor can often close on a date you pick, which helps when the house is vacant, inherited from a relative who lived elsewhere, or tied up with a tenant.

  • Broker listing: biggest pool of buyers, slowest clock, costs spelled out in the listing agreement.
  • Selling by owner: you price, show and negotiate, and a title company or attorney still has to close it.
  • Cash bid: few or no showings and a quicker closing, at a figure that accounts for repairs the buyer absorbs.

What kind of city is St. Louis for someone selling a home?

St. Louis is an independent city, which means it stands apart from St. Louis County. Wikipedia dates the split to 1877 and counts 79 officially recognized neighborhoods. That separation shapes a sale: the city ordinances, the city Recorder of Deeds and the city Collector of Revenue govern a house inside the limits, while a house across the boundary to the west falls under county and suburban rules.

Census estimates put the city at 278,144 residents in mid-2025, a drop of 7.7% from the April 2020 base. Only 45.3% of homes are lived in by their owners, so a large share of the stock is rented and many sellers are landlords or heirs. Brick defines the older housing: Laclede's Landing has cobblestone streets and brick and cast-iron warehouses, and many houses in Lafayette Square blend Greek Revival, Federal and Italianate styles.

Neighborhoods carry distinct identities. Dutchtown, Cherokee Street in Benton Park West and The Hill each have their own communities, and the Central West End sits beside the Washington University medical campus and the Cortex innovation district. Greater St. Louis is also home to seven Fortune 500 companies as of 2025, among them Centene, Emerson Electric and Edward Jones.

What happens with the occupancy inspection when a St. Louis house sells?

A sale of an occupied house triggers a new Certificate of Inspection when none has been issued in the prior 12 months. Building Division materials say 100% of the city lies inside a Housing Conservation District under Ordinance No. 71835, so the rule reaches every address in town.

The visit is a basic code check of interior and exterior conditions under the International Property Maintenance Code. The city says it is no guarantee or warranty of the building and suggests that purchasers consider a commercial grade inspection of their own. The practical details:

  • Fee: $120.00 to apply, or $200.00 if someone is found living in the dwelling without a current certificate.
  • Timing: the visit can be set for no sooner than 3 business days and no later than 15 days after the application.
  • Utilities: water and electric must be operating on inspection day.
  • Violations: when a certificate issues with violations, the owner gets 30 days to repair, and extensions can be granted for weather or other specific causes.
  • Validity: 12 months. The inspection also sets how many people may live in the unit, and no more than three unrelated persons may share a dwelling.

Apply online through the city permit portal or at City Hall, 1200 Market Street, Room 425. The Building Division answers questions at (314) 622-3313.

How do St. Louis housing figures stack up?

Survey figures for 2020 to 2024 describe a city with lower home values than the suburbs to its northwest. The middle owner-occupied value of $197,500 trails St. Charles at $298,700 and St. Peters at $269,900, though it is above St. Joseph at $154,200.

Where does a St. Louis deed get recorded?

Deeds for property in the city go to the City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds, Land Records Department, in City Hall at 1200 Market Street, Room 126. Counter hours are weekdays, 8:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m., and the land records line is (314) 622-3260. A free online search of recorded land documents lets you confirm that your own deed, an old mortgage and any lien appear the way you expect before you sign a contract.

Missouri law lets spouses convey real estate by joint deed (RSMo 442.030). Where the property is held as an estate by the entirety, both spouses are bound by the covenants in the deed, so both sign. Heirs selling an inherited house should ask the title company which probate papers it needs to see.

On the tax side, ask the St. Louis Collector of Revenue what is currently owed on your parcel before you set a closing date.

How do storms and the ground affect a St. Louis house?

Summers run hot and sticky while winters turn cold. At Lambert airport the 1991 to 2020 normals show about 41.70 inches of precipitation and 16.6 inches of snow a year, and thunderstorms occur on roughly 48 days annually. Wikipedia adds that spring storms can bring high winds, large hail and tornadoes, and that the Great Flood of 1993 is part of the region's record.

Buyers and inspectors therefore look hard at roofs, gutters, chimneys and basements. The same article notes that the area south of downtown has numerous sinkholes and caves, though most caves in the city have been sealed. A cash buyer prices these conditions in directly, while a financed buyer may ask for repairs after a home inspection.

What should a St. Louis seller do first?

Begin with paperwork, then decide how much repair work is worth doing.

  • Pull your deed and payoff statements and compare them with the Recorder of Deeds online search.
  • Find out whether a Certificate of Inspection was issued in the last 12 months. If so, a new one may not be needed.
  • Walk the exterior for violations under the property maintenance code, since the city checks outside as well as inside.
  • Make sure water and electric will be on for inspection day.
  • Line up a listing estimate, a by-owner plan and a cash bid, and compare what you would actually keep from each.

If the house is vacant, damaged or occupied by a tenant, selling as-is for cash can remove several of these steps, although the buyer still needs the Certificate of Inspection before anyone occupies the unit.

More questions about St. Louis, MO

Is an inspection required before a St. Louis house changes hands?

Yes, for an occupied house. The city requires a Certificate of Inspection when an occupied structure sells and none has been issued in the last 12 months. The application is $120.00, or $200.00 if the home is occupied without a current certificate.

How long does a St. Louis Certificate of Inspection last?

Twelve months. If violations are noted when it is issued, the owner has 30 days to correct them, with extensions possible for weather or other specific causes.

Does a house in poor shape have to be fixed before it sells in St. Louis?

Not always. The inspection is a basic code check and not a full condition report, and a cash buyer may take the house as it stands. The Certificate of Inspection is still required before anyone moves in.

Which office records the deed for a St. Louis sale?

The City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds, Land Records Department, City Hall Room 126, 1200 Market Street, phone (314) 622-3260. Your closing agent usually arranges the filing.

How many unrelated people can share a St. Louis dwelling?

No more than three. The Housing Conservation inspection also sets the number of people who may safely occupy the unit, which matters for rental properties being sold.

Where is Columbia, Missouri, and who owns homes here?

Columbia is the seat of Boone County in central Missouri, about 120 miles from both St. Louis and Kansas City and 29 miles north of Jefferson City. The July 1, 2025 Census Bureau estimate puts Columbia at 130,851 people, up from 108,500 in 2010.

It is the largest of the four Missouri cities in this series, and the only one where fewer than half of homes are owner-occupied. With the university, three hospital systems and state government nearby, many houses in town have spent time as rentals.

Columbia figures from Census QuickFacts, 2020 to 2024 estimates
MeasureColumbia

Owner-occupied housing rate48.7%
Median gross rent$1,097

Mean commute to work16.4 minutes
Adults with a bachelor's degree or higher56.7%

The city covers 66.54 square miles of land, so the value of a house depends heavily on which side of town it is on and how close it sits to the university.

How did Columbia grow from a creek-side village into a university city?

Settlers from Kentucky and Virginia moved into the Boonslick region in the early 1800s. Boone County was formed in 1820, and the first village, Smithton, struggled because wells hit bedrock. Springs along Flat Branch Creek drew the town across the creek, and Columbia was laid out in the spring of 1821 and named the county seat that year.

The city bid hard for the state university and raised three times what any rival offered. The University of Missouri sits downtown beside Stephens College and Columbia College, and education, medicine and insurance have anchored the economy since.

Hills, creek valleys and the cave systems of Rock Bridge State Park give the terrain a feel closer to the Ozarks than the northern plains. Hinkson, Perche and Flat Branch creeks run through town, so check the flood map for any house near a stream valley.

Which employers, schools and roads shape Columbia house sales?

The University of Missouri tops the 2022 list of city employers with 8,709 people, followed by University of Missouri Health Care at 5,092, Veterans United Home Loans at 3,474 and Columbia Public Schools at 2,650. The Truman Veterans' Hospital, Boone Hospital Center, the City of Columbia and Shelter Insurance also employ more than 1,000 each.

Columbia Public Schools serves almost all of the city, with four high schools: Hickman, Rock Bridge, Muriel Battle and Frederick Douglass. A very small part of the city is in the Hallsville R-IV district.

  • Interstate 70 and US 63 are the main freeways, and Routes 763, 163 (Providence Road) and 740 (Stadium Boulevard) cross the city.
  • The MKT Trail connects across town, and Columbia Regional Airport is the only commercial airport in mid-Missouri.
  • MoDOT's Improve I-70 project plans a third lane in each direction for roughly 200 miles between Blue Springs and Wentzville, with the Columbia to Kingdom City segment expected to take four to five years.

What city offices and programs help Columbia homeowners?

The city's Housing and Neighborhood Services department runs several programs that touch a house sale. Its Office of Neighborhood Services handles code enforcement at 573-817-5050, and the Housing Programs Division at 573-874-6321 runs federal and local housing aid.

  • The Homeownership Assistance Program helps make buying more affordable for eligible buyers.
  • The Home Rehab and Energy Efficiency Program brings existing homes up to property maintenance and rehabilitation standards.
  • The Neighborhood Cleanup Program supports block cleanups.

Census numbers show a mobile population. Only 77.5 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, against 88.0 percent in Blue Springs, and 11.6 percent of Columbia residents are 65 or older.

What is Columbia's weather, and how does it affect a house?

Weather swings sharply here, with a humid continental pattern. The July average is 78.5 degrees, the January average is 31 degrees, and the city sees about 35 days a year at 90 degrees or higher. Snow averages 16.5 inches a season, and spring brings the most severe weather.

Hot summers test air conditioning and attic ventilation, while freezes and storms put the pressure on roofs, gutters and older plumbing. Inspectors will check those first.

What does Columbia's Rental Unit Conservation Law mean for a seller?

Every rental unit in Columbia needs a Certificate of Compliance, and it is unlawful to operate a rental without a current one. A buyer of a former rental will want to know the certificate is valid.

  • Certificates last five years, with an inspection at each renewal.
  • Fees from January 1, 2025 are $130 for a single-family dwelling and $195 for a duplex.
  • A short-term rental unit pays a $130 application and inspection fee.
  • A certificate can be transferred after a sale within 90 days of title transfer for $15, and it carries over for the unexpired part of its term.

Applying involves an HVAC certification for gas appliances, then an inspection. Neighborhood Services at 11 N. Seventh Street, phone 573-817-5050, handles applications and transfers.

How are Boone County property taxes handled when a Columbia house sells?

The Boone County Collector mails tax statements in November, and real estate tax is due upon receipt but no later than December 31. The 2026 statements went out November 4, 2026, and the penalty-free deadline is December 31, 2026.

The collector's page explains that taxes are a lien that stays with the property, and the new owner is liable for unpaid taxes when ownership changes. Taxes are generally prorated between buyer and seller, with the buyer credited at closing for the months the seller owned the house. No money is paid to the collector at the sale itself. If you close on or after October 1, the bill may still be issued in the seller's name, and you should tell the collector the new owner's name and address.

The assessor values a house at 19 percent of its market value for tax purposes. Unpaid taxes can lead to a public tax certificate sale held on the fourth Monday in August. Boone County also has a Senior Real Estate Tax Relief Program for approved primary residences.

Where does a Columbia seller record the deed?

Deeds for Columbia addresses are filed at the Boone County Government Center, 801 East Walnut, Room 132, in Columbia. The phone number is 573-886-4345. The office records real estate documents, including deeds, deeds of trust, releases and easements, and it is the source your title company will use for a clean history of the parcel.

Property boundary maps are updated by the Assessor's office from warranty deeds the recorder receives.

What options does a Columbia seller have to sell fast?

A Columbia owner can hire an agent, go without one, or take an as-is offer from an investor. Houses with tenants in place or a lapsed rental certificate can be harder to sell on the open market, so owners of those properties often look at a direct purchase.

Gather your payoff letter, Boone County tax statement, rental certificate status and school district first. That packet lets you compare a listing's net proceeds against a cash offer without delay.

More questions about Columbia, MO

Does a Columbia rental certificate transfer to the buyer?

Yes. The city allows transfer within 90 days of title transfer for a $15 fee, and the certificate keeps its unexpired term. Call Neighborhood Services at 573-817-5050 to arrange it.

When are Boone County property taxes due?

Upon receipt of the bill, and no later than December 31. For 2026 the last day to pay without penalties and fees is December 31, 2026.

Who pays the property tax at closing?

Taxes are generally prorated, with the buyer credited by the seller for the months the seller owned the house. The collector says no tax money is paid to its office at closing.

Where is the Boone County Recorder of Deeds?

At the Boone County Government Center, 801 East Walnut, Room 132 in Columbia. Call 573-886-4345 with questions about copies or filings.

Which school district serves my Columbia house?

Almost all of the city is in Columbia Public Schools, and a very small part lies in the Hallsville R-IV district. Check the district boundary for your address.

Why is Independence called the Queen City of the Trails?

Independence earned the nickname because it was the departure point for the California, Oregon and Santa Fe Trails. Founded on March 29, 1827 and named for the Declaration of Independence, it sits on the south bank of the Missouri River and is the largest suburb on the Missouri side of the Kansas City area.

The early town thrived by outfitting emigrants. It received a home-rule charter from the Missouri General Assembly on March 8, 1849, and William McCoy became its first mayor that July. Latter Day Saint settlers arrived in 1831, Joseph Smith named a site west of the Courthouse Square for a temple, and several branches of that movement, including the Community of Christ, still base themselves in the city. Two Civil War battles were fought here, in August 1862 and October 1864.

Harry Truman grew up in Independence and returned after his presidency. The Truman Library and Museum, the Truman National Historic Site and the graves of Harry and Bess Truman are all in the city. Santa-Cali-Gon Days brings crowds each Labor Day, and the Vaile Strawberry Festival takes place on the first Saturday of June.

What does Independence's Rental Ready program require of a landlord?

Every residential rental unit in Independence must be licensed and pass a city inspection before it can be leased. The Rental Ready program started June 1, 2017, and the council expanded it in January 2025 from nine inspection items to sixteen, with the new rules taking effect on May 1, 2025.

The inspection costs $100 per dwelling unit, and a failed unit pays $60 for reinspection. Units are inspected every two years or when the tenant changes, with no more than four years between inspections. For buildings with five or more units, half the units are inspected and they cannot be the ones inspected before. Inspections must be done by a city-approved private inspector. Landlord licenses run for one year and renew annually.

Since January 1, 2026, a tenant cannot start utility service for a rental unless the landlord holds a valid, active business license. If you are selling a rental house, give the buyer your license number and your most recent inspection result.

  • The sixteen items include electrical systems, smoke detectors, handrails, plumbing fixtures, hot and cold water, GFCI outlets, egress, heating, furnaces and water heaters, and window fall protection.
  • Tenants who want the city to act must first notify the landlord, who has seven days to respond.
  • Questions go to Business and Landlord Licensing at (816) 325-7079 or blicenses@indepmo.org.

Which code violations do Independence property owners get cited for?

The Property Maintenance Division enforces Chapters 4 and 14 of the city code, and most owners get a chance to fix a problem before any penalty. Typical citations involve overgrown yards, trash and parked vehicles.

  • Grass and weeds must stay under 7 inches.
  • Trash containers come in from the curb the same day as collection and cannot go out more than 16 hours before pickup.
  • Inoperable or unlicensed vehicles belong inside a fully enclosed structure, and no vehicle may park on grass.
  • Buildings, fences, retaining walls and sidewalks must be kept in good condition.

If the deadline in a compliance order passes, the owner may face a General Ordinance Summons with fines from $100 to $500 that usually rise with repeat offenses. The city can also hire a contractor to board a structure or clear trash and weeds and charge administrative costs on top, or tow vehicles at the owner's expense. Report problems or ask questions at codes@indepmo.org. Anyone who owns property in Independence and wants to bid at Jackson County's Delinquent Land Tax Sale must first request a Code Compliance Verification, which the city emails within two business days.

Can I run a short-term rental in Independence?

Yes, with a Short-Term Rental Permit approved by the Planning Commission. No new short-term rental may sit within 500 feet of an existing one, and the city asks you to call 816-325-7823 to check your address before applying.

The application requires an evacuation plan, a floor plan and a parking plan, plus a fee paid online. Operators report and remit the transient guest tax to the city every month. Temporary rules for the 2026 FIFA World Cup applied from June 1 through July 30, 2026, and that period is over. Buyers who plan to run a short-term rental should ask the city whether an existing permit transfers with the house.

How do taxes and recording work across the Jackson and Clay county line?

Your parcel's county decides who bills the tax and records the deed, and most Independence addresses are in Jackson County. If your property sits in the small Clay County portion, the Clay County Collector and Recorder of Deeds handle it.

Jackson County levies real estate tax annually, due December 31, and the postmark decides timeliness: a check mailed and postmarked on December 29 counts as on time. The county assessor sets the value, and the bill equals the taxable value divided by 100 and multiplied by the levy rate. Commercial property is assessed at 32% and agricultural property at 12%, against 19% for residential.

For recording, the Jackson County Recorder of Deeds charges $20 for a certified death certificate copy, which estate sales often need, and $3 for a state or federal tax lien. A deed costs $23 for the first page. Individual personal property is handled at the Truman Courthouse, 112 W. Lexington, on the first floor in Independence. Real property valuation is at 1300 Washington Street in Kansas City.

Which school districts and employers influence the Independence market?

Four public school districts overlap the city: Independence, Blue Springs, Fort Osage and Raytown. Which district your street belongs to matters, so confirm it before you list. Independence has three public high schools and four public middle schools, among them Bridger, Pioneer Ridge, Bingham and Nowlin. Blue River Community College and a Graceland University campus are in the city.

The largest employers in the 2016 city financial report were the Independence School District with 2,200 employees, Northrop Grumman Innovation Systems with 1,722, Centerpoint Medical Center with 1,400, the city with 1,097 and the Government Employee Health Association with 743. Independence Power and Light, a city-owned electric utility founded in 1901, serves customers in town.

Landmarks include the National Frontier Trails Museum, the Truman Library, the Midwest Genealogy Center and the old Jackson County Courthouse, which was modeled on Philadelphia's Independence Hall.

More questions about Independence, MO

What do landlords need in Independence?

It licenses and inspects them. Landlords need a business license, a Rental Ready inspection every two years at $100 per unit, and since January 1, 2026 a valid license is required before utilities can start for a tenant.

Which county handles my Independence property taxes?

Jackson County for most addresses and Clay County for the small portion of the city that extends into it. Check your tax statement to see which collector sent it.

What are the common code problems on an Independence house?

Tall grass over 7 inches, trash containers left at the curb, unlicensed vehicles parked outside and deteriorated fences or sidewalks. Fines for a summons range from $100 to $500.

Can I list my Independence house as a short-term rental?

Only with a city permit approved by the Planning Commission, and no new rental may be within 500 feet of another. Operators remit transient guest tax monthly.

Is Independence growing or shrinking?

Slightly shrinking. The Census Bureau estimate for July 1, 2025 is 121,675, which is 1.0% below the 2020 base of 122,954.

How can I sell a house quickly in Lee's Summit, MO?

Three paths exist for a Lee's Summit homeowner: hire a listing agent, sell on your own, or take an as-is cash offer. Speed usually comes down to the condition of the house and whether the title is clean.

A tidy house in a settled subdivision may sell on a normal listing in a few weeks. A house with a failing roof, a stack of Neighborhood Services notices or a tenant who has stopped answering the door tends to stall once buyers read the inspection report. For those houses, a buyer who pays cash and skips the repair list can move sooner, though you should expect the offer to sit below what a polished listing might reach.

  • Agent listing: the widest buyer pool and usually the best price, paid for with prep time, showings and a commission.

What should a seller know about the city of Lee's Summit?

Lee's Summit is a Kansas City suburb in Jackson County, and part of it extends into Cass County. It borders Kansas City on the west and northwest, Independence on the north, and Greenwood and Lake Winnebago to the southeast and south.

The town started in 1865 as Strother, a stop that William Bullitt Howard platted along the Missouri Pacific tracks, and it took the name Lee's Summit in 1868. It became a fourth-class city in 1877. Postwar highways and demand for single family homes turned the farm community into a commuter suburb, and the New Longview neighborhood, built in 2004, now covers part of the old Longview Farm estate.

Downtown is a ten-block by ten-block district on the National Register of Historic Places, ringed mostly by single family streets. Interstate 470, U.S. Route 50 and Missouri Route 291 make a triangle of highways around the center, with Route 150 crossing the south side. Six large reservoirs lie in and around the city, among them Longview Lake and Raintree Lake. The biggest employers are the Lee's Summit R-VII School District, the federal National Benefits Center, GEHA, University Health Lakewood Medical Center and John Knox Village, and about 80 percent of residents commuted outside the city as of 2015.

That commuter profile shapes marketing. Buyers often ask how long the drive to downtown Kansas City or Overland Park will take, so a listing that names the nearest on-ramp helps.

When you list, name the district in the first line of the description. Two houses a few blocks apart can feed different schools, and families ask before they book a showing. The county assessor or your agent can confirm the district for a specific address.

How does Neighborhood Services handle code cases that could affect a sale?

Neighborhood Services opens a case when someone files a complaint, often through the free LS Connect app or website. An open case does not prevent a sale, but a buyer's lender or inspector may ask about it.

The city describes the sequence this way:

  • An inspector visits within five business days of the complaint.
  • If a violation exists, a notice goes to the owner or tenant, typically giving 10 days to correct it.
  • A re-inspection follows when that window closes, and a courtesy extension is sometimes granted.
  • Leftover grass and some rubbish are cleared by a city contractor, and the owner pays for it.
  • Cases still unresolved go to the Prosecutor's Office, which seeks a court summons.

For an inherited or vacant house, walk the exterior before you list. Mow, clear trash containers from view and repair fence sections. If you suspect a complaint was filed while you were away, call Development Services at 816.969.1200 and ask whether a case exists on the address.

Are short-term rentals allowed in Lee's Summit?

Yes, within limits. A short-term rental needs a business license, and the city restricts where one may operate.

Under the city's rules, a rental of this kind belongs inside the Old Town Master Development Plan area, which is east of US Highway 50, west of Route 291 North and south of Chipman Road. Outside Old Town, the parcel must exceed one acre. Only single-family houses and duplexes qualify, and the owner or a local representative has to occupy a unit on the same or an adjacent parcel.

For a seller, that means an Airbnb buyer will check the address against those boundaries first. If your house sits on a standard lot outside Old Town, market it to owner-occupants and long-term landlords.

Where are deeds recorded and when is the property tax due on a Lee's Summit house?

The deed goes to the recorder of deeds in the county where the parcel lies, and the yearly tax bill is payable by December 31. Because Lee's Summit sits in both Jackson and Cass counties, find out which one holds your parcel before you plan closing.

Jackson County's Recorder of Deeds requires the first page of a deed to show the document title, its date, every grantor with marital status, every grantee, any statutory addresses and the legal description, all beneath a three-inch top margin. A title company normally prepares and records the deed. If you draft one yourself, match that layout.

Jackson County posted its 2026 real estate and personal property bills online on November 3, 2026, with payment due on or before December 31, 2026. Residential property is assessed at 19 percent of market value. The tax equals the taxable value divided by 100, times the levy rate for your taxing districts. The Collection Department cannot lower an assessment or a levy, so direct valuation questions to the assessor. Your parcel's share in Cass County, if any, is billed by that county's collector.

What commonly delays a Lee's Summit closing?

A handful of problems cause most delays, and you can check for each of them before you pick a buyer.

  • A deed still in the name of a deceased relative, or a lien that was never released.
  • An unresolved Neighborhood Services notice or unpaid mowing charge.
  • An occupant who has not agreed to a move-out date.
  • Structural or water problems that an inspector will flag.

Knowing which apply lets you set a realistic closing date. Buyers who purchase as-is, including cash buyers, are often more comfortable taking on several of these than a buyer who relies on a mortgage appraisal.

More questions about Lee's Summit, MO

Does an open code violation stop me from selling in Lee's Summit?

No. A notice from Neighborhood Services does not bar a sale, though buyers will ask about it. The city typically gives 10 days to correct a violation, so a quick cleanup often closes the case. Development Services at 816.969.1200 can tell you whether a case is open.

Do I record my deed in Jackson County or Cass County?

It depends on the parcel. Most of the city lies in Jackson County, yet a portion extends into Cass County. Your title company or the county assessor can confirm where your address falls.

What is the deadline for the 2026 property tax bill on a Jackson County home?

December 31, 2026. Jackson County put the bills online on November 3, 2026. Your closing agent can show how the year's tax will be divided with the buyer.

Can an investor run a short-term rental in a Lee's Summit house?

Only in the Old Town Master Development Plan area or on a parcel larger than one acre, and only in a single-family house or duplex. A business license is required, and the owner or a local representative must live on the same or an adjacent parcel.

How quickly can a cash sale of a Lee's Summit house close?

Often faster than a financed sale, because no lender appraisal is involved. The calendar still depends on title work, so a deed that needs a probate filing or a lien release will take longer than a clean one.

How do homeowners usually sell in St. Charles, MO?

Sellers here tend to choose between a broker's listing, a sale they run themselves, and an investor paying cash. The right pick turns on how much work the house needs, how soon you must close, and how you feel about open houses.

What is St. Charles like, and why should a seller care?

The city is the seat of St. Charles County, set on the Missouri River just above its junction with the Mississippi, roughly 20 miles northwest of downtown St. Louis. A French-Canadian trader, Louis Blanchette, settled it around 1769 as Les Petites Cotes, and Wikipedia ranks it third among the oldest cities in present-day Missouri. It served as the first state capital from 1821 to 1826, and the First Missouri State Capitol is now a state historic site.

Older blocks around Main Street and the riverfront make up the St. Charles Historic District, where shops and restaurants share streets with homes. Farther out, building since the late 1970s produced the subdivisions that form most of the housing stock. The eastern end of the Katy Trail is nearby, and the Christmas Traditions Festival fills the historic streets from the day after Thanksgiving until the Saturday after Christmas.

Roads are a strength: Interstate 70 and Missouri routes 370, 94 and 364 all serve the city, and Wikipedia reports that, according to the Federal Highway Administration, St. Charles was the site of the first interstate highway project, a claim Kansas and Pennsylvania also make. Lindenwood University sits on Kingshighway near downtown.

Which school districts serve St. Charles homes?

The City of St. Charles School District covers most addresses, with six elementary schools, two middle schools and two high schools, St. Charles High and St. Charles West. Southern edges of town belong to Francis Howell, while Orchard Farm serves the north.

Families shop by district, so learn which one applies to your street before you write a listing description. A call to the district office settles the assignment for a given house number.

What does the city of St. Charles require from sellers?

Sellers must complete and sign a city disclosure on every residential real estate transaction inside St. Charles, under Ordinance 23-062, passed June 6, 2023 and in force since September 1, 2023. After closing, a notarized copy goes to the city. The disclosure does not need to be recorded.

The form gives incoming owners formal notice of local rules. The city lists these topics:

  • Building and sign permits, inspections and fencing
  • RV and boat parking and storage
  • Property maintenance and solid waste collection
  • Short term rentals
  • Historic preservation districts and floodplain development
  • Site plan review, architectural review and zoning classification

Ask your title company to place the disclosure in the closing packet so it is not forgotten. City staff take questions at 636-949-3222.

Rentals have their own rule. Residential occupancy inspections are required for all long term rentals, with an approved inspection before the first tenant moves in and between each change of tenant. If the house has been rented out, ask Community Development whether the unit's inspection is current.

Can a St. Charles house operate as a short term rental?

Rarely, and no longer in most residential areas of the city. On April 15, 2025 the city amended its ordinance, lifting the moratorium but limiting new residential permits to the Extended Historic Preservation District and cutting the cap to 0.15% of housing units, or up to 48 units in residential zones. The city reports that it is at the maximum and is not accepting new applications for residentially zoned short term rentals.

Existing permits renew every year and include a safety inspection, a noise monitoring device, one off-street parking space per rented bedroom and a 500 foot buffer from other residential short term rentals. Commercially zoned properties inside the historic district overlay are treated differently. If a house has operated as a short term rental, ask Community Development to confirm its permit at 636-949-3222, and ask the county at 636-949-7900 how the use affects the tax bill.

Where is a St. Charles deed recorded, and at what price?

The county Recorder of Deeds, at 201 N. Second Street in St. Charles, files deeds for city properties. The office takes cards for a convenience fee and refuses personal checks.

Closing agents usually file the deed and pay from settlement funds. Phone 636-949-7900 if you plan to record something on your own, like a release of an old lien.

Weather is the last thing to plan around. Wikipedia's climate summary describes humid subtropical conditions, with spring the wettest season. Check gutters, basements and the roof before inspections, particularly near the river or in the floodplain, where the city's disclosure list also flags development rules.

What should a St. Charles seller line up before accepting an offer?

Get the local paperwork moving early, because the city disclosure and the county recording both sit on the closing timeline.

  • Download the disclosure form from the city's Residential Real Estate Disclosure page and complete it with your title company.
  • Work out whether the house is in the historic district, a floodplain or a residential zone, since each carries its own rules.
  • If the house has been rented, check the long term rental inspection status.
  • Confirm the school district for the address and note it in your marketing.
  • If the house hosted short term guests, ask the county how that affects the tax bill.

With 30,362 households and a population up 2.7% since the 2020 base, St. Charles is growing, and a tidy file helps whichever route you choose.

Does the city of St. Charles require a seller disclosure?

Yes. Ordinance 23-062 has applied to all residential transactions inside city limits since September 1, 2023. The seller signs the form, a notarized copy goes to the city after closing, and it is not recorded.

What is the St. Charles County deed recording fee?

Since August 28, 2026 the county charges $23.00 for page one and $3.00 for every page after it, and $25.00 more when a document is non-standard.

Most of the city is in the City of St. Charles School District. Southern edges belong to Francis Howell and northern areas to Orchard Farm, so confirm your address with the district office.

Can I turn my St. Charles house into an Airbnb before selling it?

Probably not in a residential zone. The city is at its cap of 0.15% of housing units and is not taking new applications for residentially zoned short term rentals. Call 636-949-3222 to verify zoning.

Do I need an occupancy inspection to sell my St. Charles home?

The city's inspection page ties occupancy inspections to long term rentals, which need one before the first tenant and between tenants. For an owner-occupied sale, call Community Development at 636-949-3222 to confirm.

St. Joseph is the seat of Buchanan County, on the Missouri River in the northwest corner of the state, about 30 miles north of Kansas City. Joseph Robidoux, a fur trader, founded it, and it was incorporated in 1843. Wikipedia says it was the westernmost point reachable by rail until after the Civil War, and that it was an endpoint of the Pony Express from April 1860 to late October 1861. Wikipedia notes that the downtown portion of I-229 is slated to be demolished and replaced with a surface boulevard, so ask the city about plans if your house sits near that corridor.

Does St. Joseph have rules for rental houses and inspections?

The city's application materials list an inspection fee of $50.00 for each inspection performed by a city inspector, and rentals also need a business license. Forms go to the Housing Compliance Inspection Office, 1100 Frederick Avenue, City Hall Room 107.

The name comes from a spring on a hillside that feeds a tributary of the Little Blue River. Freighters on the Santa Fe route used it as a stopping point as early as 1825, and settler Franklin Smith arrived from Virginia in 1838 and opened the first post office in 1845.

In March 1878 the Chicago and Alton Railroad announced a station about a mile east, and the town moved its center to follow the tracks. The county court approved incorporation on September 7, 1880. The city became a fourth-class city in 1904 and adopted a home rule charter in April 1994.

Building permits come from the Codes Administration Division of Community Development at 903 W. Main Street, phone 816-228-0118. The city moved to the 2024 International Residential and Building Codes on June 1, 2026. Applications filed before that date follow the older codes, and permitted projects keep the code in force when the permit was issued.

Jackson County bills real estate tax each year and the bill is due December 31, using the postmark to decide whether a mailed payment is on time. Interest, penalties and fees apply to anything paid after that date.

The county explains the math this way: houses are assessed at 19 percent of what the assessor thinks they would sell for, and the tax is the taxable value divided by 100 and multiplied by the combined levy rate of the school district, city, fire district and other taxing bodies. Blue Springs owners have three paths: an agent's listing, a private sale, or a direct purchase by an investor. No, the 2026 Board of Equalization window ended July 13, 2026. Contact the Assessment office about the next value notice and keep an appraisal or sale paperwork ready for the next filing window.

Only when structural roof decking is replaced, according to the Codes Administration Division. Repairs over 10 percent of the roof area in a three year span are treated as a full roof covering replacement under the updated code.

Yes, with city registration and a business license. The operator needs a local responsible agent, must respect occupancy and quiet hour limits, and files monthly lodging tax returns. Call Business Services at 816-228-0131 for the packet.

Under RSMo 442.380, any written instrument that conveys land goes on record with that county's recorder. For Jefferson City that is the Cole County Recorder of Deeds at 311 E. High St., Room 101, phone 573-634-9115. The office keeps a general index back to 1821 and full digital indexing from July 1983 to today.

The county fee table lists $26 for the first page of a standard document and $3 for each added page, after a statewide $2 increase under Missouri SB 938 that took effect August 28, 2026. Copies cost $1 per page plus $1 for certification. The recorder warns that private mailers offering deed copies often charge $80 or more, so order copies from the office itself. Copies of transfer deeds also go to the Cole County Assessor.

Ask the Building Division at 573-634-6410 whether your address needs anything before closing. Permits are required for additions, decks, garages, fences, pools and electrical or plumbing changes, and a Certificate of Completion closes out the work.

Where do I record the deed after a Jefferson City sale?

Record it with the Cole County Recorder of Deeds at 311 E. High St., Room 101, unless your parcel lies in the Callaway County portion of the city, in which case ask the title company. Statute 442.380 sends the recording to the recorder of the parcel's county.

What if my Jefferson City property is a rental?

Make sure it is registered with the city. Registration is free and must be renewed between January 1 and January 31 each year. If ownership changes, the form that reports no changes does not apply, so send Planning and Protective Services the full registration.

Yes, but resolve it first when you can. Notices go to the owner address on file with the Cole County Assessor. If the city abates a nuisance, the cost becomes a special tax bill on the property plus a $270 administrative fee, which a buyer or title company will want settled.

How did the river and the railroad shape Cape Girardeau?

A French trader named Jean Pierre Girardeau set up a post on a rocky bluff in the early 1760s, and the city takes its name from that cape. Louis Lorimier founded the community on January 4, 1793, under a Spanish land grant. The town was platted in 1806, incorporated in 1808 and made a city by the legislature in 1843.

Steamboats made it the largest port on the Mississippi between St. Louis and Memphis. The first railroad arrived in the early 1880s, and the city's population more than doubled between 1900 and 1920. The International Shoe Company factory built in 1907 gave the Red Star neighborhood its name, because many workers lived nearby.

Floods from the Mississippi hit the riverfront repeatedly between 1927 and 1951. The Army Corps of Engineers finished a floodwall and levee of more than a mile in 1964, and the city now owns and maintains it. The city's online maps include a flood zone layer, which is the place to check a parcel near the river.

Health care leads. St. Francis Medical Center employs about 3,143 people and Mercy Hospital Southeast about 2,950. Procter & Gamble, Southeast Missouri State University, Cape Girardeau Public Schools, Drury Hotels and Century Casino complete the list of large local employers.

The city is mostly in the Cape Girardeau Public Schools district, with a section of Cape Girardeau County in the Jackson R-II district. A small part of the city lies in Scott County, where Scott City R-I covers most of that area. Check your parcel before you tell a buyer which district applies.

Cape Girardeau sits in the humid subtropical zone. Average yearly precipitation is about 47.9 inches, spring is the wettest season, and the record high is 107 degrees on June 29, 2012. The airport sees about 47 days a year at 90 degrees or hotter.

Standards include working smoke alarms in every bedroom, in the hallway outside bedrooms and on each floor, bedroom egress windows with a clear opening of at least 24 inches high and 30 inches wide, handrails on steps with four or more risers, and guards on landings more than 30 inches high.

For repair work, inspection requests received after 11:30 a.m. are scheduled for the next day, final inspections need 24 hours notice, and approved plans must be on site. Cape Girardeau became a constitutional home rule city in 1982 with a council-manager form of government, and voters adopted ward representation in 1993. City Hall moved to 44 N. Lorimier Street in 2022, where the Common Pleas Courthouse and the Carnegie Library were joined into one building.

How do Cape Girardeau County assessments and taxes work?

The county assessor, whose office is at 1 Barton Square, Suite 201 in Jackson, values every parcel. State law requires reassessment of existing real property as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year, and new improvements are added when construction finishes.

Tax rates come from the school, library, fire and other districts, not from the assessor. The assessor's website has a real estate search and parcel map, and the office handles the Missouri Property Tax Credit form 948 for qualifying seniors and disabled owners. Call 573-243-2468 or email appraisal@capecounty.us for value questions.

Ask the Cape Girardeau County Collector for your current bill, and ask your closing agent how the year gets divided.

How is a deed recorded in Cape Girardeau County?

Deeds go to the county Recorder of Deeds at #1 Barton Square, Suite 203, Jackson, phone 573-243-8123, with weekday hours of 8:00 to 4:30. Documents can be mailed, dropped off or e-recorded.

The recording fee for a standard document is $24 on page one plus $3 per added page, and a document that misses the formatting standards carries an extra $25. Pages must be 8.5 by 11 inches, with a three inch margin on the first page left blank for the recorder's stamp. The office cannot create documents or give legal advice, so an attorney or title agent drafts the deed.

What are the ways to sell a Cape Girardeau house fast?

Cape Girardeau owners can hire an agent, go it alone, or ask investors for direct offers. In a market with many renters and a lower price range, houses that need work or carry tenants can sit on the market, so some owners prefer a quick as-is sale.

Mostly it is in Cape Girardeau County, but a small part of the city lies in Scott County. Check the parcel's county before calling an assessor or recorder.

Where does a Cape Girardeau deed get filed?

The Cape Girardeau County Recorder of Deeds in Jackson, at #1 Barton Square, Suite 203. A standard deed costs $24 on page one plus $3 per extra page, plus $25 if formatting rules are not met.

State law requires reassessment as of January 1 of every odd-numbered year. The assessor also adds new improvements as construction finishes, so a remodel can change the value in any year.

The city requires residential rental licensing and inspects against a safety checklist. Call Inspection Services at 573-339-6327 to confirm your unit's status, since buyers who plan to keep tenants will ask.

Houses near the Mississippi River depend on the floodwall and levee built in 1964. The city publishes interactive maps with flood zone layers, so check your parcel there.

The checklist follows the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code plus ordinances adopted by Maryland Heights and St. Louis County. Read it before you schedule and fix the easy items first.

How should I time the inspection, the permit and the closing?

Treat the inspection as the first date on the calendar and work forward from it. A passed inspection starts a 90-day window for the new occupant's permit, so a closing that slips past that window can mean a second inspection.

  • Week one: submit the inspection application and photo ID, then pick up the appointment time the city gives you.
  • Inspection day: arrange for the owner, agent or another named representative to be on site, since lockbox entry is refused.
  • If a Field Correction Notice is issued: fix the items and request the re-inspection. Two re-inspections are covered by the $75 fee.
  • Before closing: the buyer submits the permit application with the sales contract or other closing document as proof of ownership.

The Building Division at (314) 291-6550 can answer scheduling questions. Both sides benefit when the buyer's agent and the seller's agent agree early on who applies.

Which homes does the city inspect when ownership changes?

The rule covers any residential premises, not just houses. Existing multi-family complexes are inspected at a change of ownership, and each apartment is inspected when a new tenant moves in.

Special cases may qualify for a temporary occupancy permit at the building commissioner's discretion, and Jason Boren's office at (314) 738-2241 takes those requests. A seller who owns a small investment building should check which category applies before setting a closing date.

What does Maryland Heights look like to a buyer?

Maryland Heights is a second-ring suburb west-northwest of St. Louis in St. Louis County. It was incorporated in 1985, and the city is a third-class statutory city run by a mayor and an eight-member council elected from four wards.

The city covers 23.35 square miles, including 1.52 square miles of water. It regulates development in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, requires a floodplain development permit for any work there, and participates in the National Flood Insurance Program. Its floodplain administrator can say on request whether a property is inside the hazard area and can share the flood zone and base flood elevation shown on the map. Ask for that before you list, because flood insurance is one of the first questions a buyer raises.

Employment is a strong draw. The city's 2022 financial report named Spectrum Mid West, World Wide Technology, Edward Jones, Magellan Health Services and Hollywood Casino St. Louis as its top employers. The Parkway and Pattonville school districts serve the city, and both received Distinction in Performance recognition from the Missouri Department of Education. The population jumped from 5,676 in 1980 to 25,407 in 1990 after incorporation, and reached 28,284 by the 2020 census.

A renter needs the same occupancy permit as a buyer, since the city requires one at any change of tenancy. Short-term rentals such as Airbnb have a separate city page and a Short-Term Rental Application.

For a seller who is keeping the house as a rental, this has a practical effect: every time a tenant moves out, an inspection is due before the next one moves in. Selling to a buyer who intends to own the house removes the repeated inspection cycle for you.

How are the deed and property tax handled in St. Louis County?

Deeds are recorded with the St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds in Clayton, and property tax is billed by the county's Collector of Revenue with payment due by December 31.

The recording fee is $26 for the first page and $3 for each added page, with a $25 extra charge when a document does not meet Missouri formatting standards. A mailed deed goes to the Recorder of Deeds at 41 S Central Ave, Clayton, MO 63105, with a check made payable to ROD. If you use eRecording, the vendor may add its own fees.

Property tax must be paid or postmarked by December 31 of the billing year. After that date, interest of up to 18 percent a year and a 2 percent penalty can apply under Missouri law. The Collector's customer portal offers payment plans on delinquent bills. If you sell before the bill arrives, ask your title company how the year's tax will be divided.

Yes, an inspection and occupancy permit are required at any change of ownership. The seller, an agent, a property manager or a power of attorney can apply for the inspection, which costs $75 and includes up to two re-inspections.

How long is the Maryland Heights inspection good for?

Once the house passes, the new occupant has 90 days to obtain the occupancy permit. After that, a new inspection may be required, so line up the closing date with the permit window.

The city regulates development in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area and participates in the National Flood Insurance Program. Its floodplain administrator can tell you whether a specific property is in or out of the zone.

What does it cost to record a deed in St. Louis County?

$26 for the first page and $3 for each additional page, plus $25 if the document does not meet Missouri formatting standards. A title company usually records it for you.

How did Gladstone become its own city, and why does that matter to a seller?

Gladstone exists as a separate city because its residents voted in November 1952 to incorporate and avoid annexation by Kansas City. The area had been known as Linden, and the city today is a Clay County suburb roughly 10 to 20 minutes from downtown Kansas City and from Kansas City International Airport.

The city is a third-class city under state statute with a council-manager government. Five council members are elected every three years on staggered terms, and a city manager runs daily operations.

On a map, Gladstone is a rough rectangle running from about NE 55th and Englewood Road on the south to NE 77th on the north, and from N. Jackson Avenue to N. Broadway. A panhandle reaches south to NW 44th Street. Missouri Routes 1 and 283 connect the city to North Kansas City and Kansas City, U.S. 169 sits less than 1.5 miles off the western border, and I-29 passes near the southern tip. How do Clay County taxes, prepayments and recording work for a Gladstone sale?

Gladstone sits in Clay County, so the county collector bills your real estate tax and the county Recorder of Deeds files your deed. Bills normally go out by mid-November, Missouri statutes require payment by December 31 whether or not one arrived, and the county asks anyone without a bill by November 30 to call 816-407-3200.

A payment postmarked after December 31 draws a one-time 9% penalty and interest of 1.5% per month on the unpaid balance. External drop boxes stay open around the clock, and deposits before midnight on December 31 count as on time.   • Delays tied to the senior program pushed some 2025 bills out later than usual.
  • Check the billing portal for the parcel before listing to confirm the prior year is paid.

Which schools, parks and employers influence buyers in Gladstone?

The North Kansas City School District serves Gladstone. Elementary boundaries that reach into the city include Chapel Hill, Linden West, Meadowbrook and Oakwood Manor. Most of Gladstone is zoned to Antioch Middle School, which is inside the city. High school assignment varies: most addresses feed Oak Park High School in Kansas City, while the portion south of NW Englewood Road feeds Northgate Middle School and North Kansas City High School. Gladstone also has a branch of the Mid-Continent Public Library, and Metropolitan Community College counts the North Kansas City district in its taxation area.

Maple Woods Natural Area, a remnant of the mesic forest that once covered the site, is a National Natural Landmark inside the city. The Atkins-Johnson Farmhouse Property joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2007.

The city's top employers in its 2016 financial report were Walmart with 354 workers, the North Kansas City School District with 335, Hy-Vee with 280 and the city itself with 196.

What are the realistic ways to sell a house in Gladstone?

Three paths cover most sales here, and the right one depends on repair needs, timing and how much of the process you want to manage yourself.

  • A direct investor purchase suits a house with deferred work, tenants, or an estate that needs a fast and quiet close. The buyer takes the house in its current condition.
  • A for-sale-by-owner approach suits a seller comfortable handling contracts, disclosures and city paperwork alone.

Compare each offer by what you take home after tax proration, any lien payoff, title charges and recording. Ask every buyer who pays closing costs, how long they need and whether the offer depends on a loan.

If the house is behind on payments, read the city's Beware of Foreclosure Rescue Scams brochure before you sign anything with a stranger who offers to take over the loan. Call your lender first to learn your options, and speak with an attorney if you want legal advice on a deed or contract.

Community Development lists a Residential Sale Permit Application and a Planning a Residential Sale brochure. Call (816) 423-4111 to learn which steps apply to your sale before you accept an offer.

Clay County. The Recorder of Deeds can be reached at 816-407-3550 or recorder@claycountymo.gov for the current fee schedule and document standards.

A payment postmarked after December 31 carries a one-time 9% penalty plus 1.5% interest per month on the unpaid balance.

Tell your title company before closing. Prepayments are held in a separate account, applied to the annual bill in late October, and refunded only after billing files are complete.

Slowly. The Census Bureau estimate for July 1, 2025 is 27,497, up 1.6% from the April 2020 base of 27,058.

Put the elementary school name in your listing, since young families search by school.

What is Nixa's rental inspection rule, and does it affect a sale?

Nixa requires a rental unit that is at least one year old to pass an inspection before a new tenant moves in and before utilities go into the tenant's name. It matters to a seller when the buyer plans to rent the house out.

  • Fee: $25 per inspection, paid before the visit through a link the city emails after you submit the request form.
  • Notice: 24 hours; same-day inspections are not available. Inspections run 8:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, in a morning or afternoon window.
  • Who can schedule: only a landlord or property manager.
  • Penalty: $50 if a tenant moves in, or receives keys, before a passed inspection. An early move-in inspection costs $75.
  • Failed inspection: 90 days to make repairs and call for a re-inspection, after which a new inspection and $25 fee apply.

The house must be empty, clean and move-in ready. The inspector looks at the roof and gutters, smoke detectors on every story, GFCI protection in bathrooms, water heater safety valves, the windows and doors, weeds above 12 inches and other items on the city's checklist. Planning and Development answers questions at (417) 725-5850.

Can I run a short-term rental in Nixa?

Nixa regulates short-term residential rentals in its code, and the rules changed after Missouri House Bill 1662 took effect in June 2022. Ask Planning and Development which version applies before you advertise one.

According to a May 2024 staff report, the city's first ordinance dated from August 2019 and allowed such rentals only in a primary residence with a special use permit. Staff proposed two categories: a primary residence rental, which needs only a city business license, and a non-primary residence rental, which would be subject to a ban on using accessory structures, an annual rental inspection and a 150-foot separation from other short-term rentals. Anyone buying an investment house for this use should ask the city whether the proposal was adopted as written.

How do Christian County records and taxes work for a Nixa sale?

Christian County keeps the land records, and its Recorder of Deeds office is in the Historical Courthouse at 100 W. Church Street, Room 104, in Ozark. A title company ordinarily records the deed after closing.

The office takes walk-in, mail and electronic filings, with eRecording routed through a vendor such as iCounty Technologies. Staff cannot supply forms, notarize or give legal advice. Missouri Senate Bill 938 adjusted recording fees on August 28, 2026, so ask the office for the present charge. A free service at deedwatch.com emails an owner whenever a document is recorded under a registered name.

The assessor covers 564 square miles holding over 42,951 real estate parcels, and the county's total assessed value passed $2 billion for 2025. Homes are assessed at 19 percent of market value, and the levy comes from thirteen school districts, eight road districts, ten cities, nine fire districts and other bodies, so the districts at your address set your bill. Ask the Collector's Office in Room 101 of the courthouse for the amount and due date. The county also announced a Senior Citizen Real Estate Tax Credit: first-time applications open March 1, 2027 and close June 15, 2027 for owners who are at least 62 by December 31, 2026 and who have lived in the home since at least June 29, 2026 and have paid their 2026 taxes.

More questions about Nixa, MO

Does Nixa inspect a house when it is sold?

Only if the buyer plans to rent it out. Nixa's program inspects rental units before each new tenant moves in, for $25, and a landlord cannot let a tenant move in until the unit has passed.

What is the penalty if a tenant moves into a Nixa rental before it passes inspection?

$50. An early move-in inspection costs $75. A landlord who allows more than one violation can be summoned to Municipal Court.

Where do I record a deed for a house in Nixa?

At the Christian County Recorder of Deeds in the Historical Courthouse at 100 W. Church Street, Room 104, in Ozark. Your title company can file it for you.

Can I run an Airbnb in my Nixa house?

Possibly. Nixa has short-term rental rules that were rewritten after Missouri House Bill 1662. A primary residence rental needs a city business license, and the rules for other houses may add an annual inspection and a 150-foot spacing requirement. Confirm the current version with Planning and Development.

How do I set up utilities after buying a house in Nixa?

The buyer opens an account with Nixa Utilities at 715 W Mt Vernon St with a residential application, photo ID, information on every adult living there and a deposit. Rental properties also need a passed rental inspection.

Belton at a glance

What slows down or speeds up a Belton house sale?

Belton owners can list with an agent, sell without one or take a cash offer, and condition and tenancy usually decide which. The city's rental program, plus Cass County's role in tax and recording, shape the calendar, so line those pieces up early.

Rental houses catch people off guard. Since January 1, 2025, each rental unit inside the city limits must be registered, and the city inspects between tenants. A landlord selling, or a buyer who plans to lease the place out, should read that program before setting a closing date.

Where is Belton, and who lives there?

Belton is a city in northwestern Cass County that belongs to the Kansas City metro area. It sits four miles from the Kansas border on Missouri Route 58, west of I-49 and U.S. 71. Raymore is four miles east, Peculiar is seven miles southeast and Grandview, in Jackson County, is five miles north. The city covers 14.25 square miles of land at about 1,099 feet in elevation.

Belton was platted in 1871 and probably took its name from surveyor Capt. Marcus Lindsey Belt, and its post office has run since 1872. Growth came after World War II. The census counted 1,233 residents in 1950, 4,897 in 1960 and 12,270 in 1970, and the 2020 count was 23,953. Its July 1, 2025 estimate is 26,193. The 2020 median age was 36.1, and 7.7 percent of the 9,936 housing units stood empty.

Belton School District #124 serves most of town with six elementary schools, two middle schools and Belton High School, while part of eastern Belton belongs to the Raymore-Peculiar district. Metropolitan Community College levies tax in the Belton district, and the Cass County Public Library has a branch here.

What do Belton homes and rents look like?

Renters make up a large share of Belton, which helps explain the city's rental program. Survey estimates for 2020 to 2024 show owners in 59 percent of homes, with a midpoint value of $203,200.

What are Belton's rental registration and code enforcement rules?

All rental units inside Belton must be registered, and inspections happen between tenants, after one leaves and before the next moves in. The program took effect on January 1, 2025, under an ordinance the council approved on October 10, 2023.

  • Registration costs $20 per unit and renews every 12 months.
  • A $50 late fee applies to each 30-day period a registration is past due.
  • An inspection done after the tenant has already moved in costs $20.
  • Reinspection fees begin after two failed inspections and are $20 each.

Write to rental@belton.org to book an inspection or ask about the program. Neighborhood Improvement and Code Enforcement, a division of Community Development, enforces the property maintenance and use ordinances. Since October 28, 2024, active violations show on the city's eTRAKiT portal, where a public account lets you view them, apply for permits and schedule inspections. Look up your own address there before you take an offer.

Can I run a short-term rental in Belton?

Only with city approval, and the rules are tight. The council passed Ordinance 2025-4950 on November 25, 2025, and each short-term rental now needs a registration plus a special use permit. The staff report lists a $70 annual registration fee, a $50 inspection fee and a $150 permit fee, at least $270 to begin.

Occupancy is capped at two adults per bedroom plus one more adult per dwelling, with ten guests the ceiling, children included. Hosts remit the city's 5 percent hotel and motel tax monthly, and nobody may register more than five units. The staff report described sites limited to the Old Town Belton area and parcels over three acres, so ask Community Development how the location rule applies to your address.

A temporary carve-out for the 2026 FIFA World Cup covered only June 1 through July 31, 2026, and it expired on August 1, 2026. Operating outside the rules draws fines of $200 to $500, and every day can count as its own offense. A buyer who wants a Belton short-term rental should get the city's answer before closing.

How do Cass County taxes work when I sell in Belton?

Cass County bills real estate once a year, in November, and expects payment on receipt and by December 31, judged by U.S. postmark. Penalties and fees can climb to 25 percent in the first delinquent year. Houses are assessed at 19 percent of market value, and the levy rate is applied per hundred dollars of that assessed figure.

The county's guide for buyers and sellers tells the new owner to pay the full bill by December 31, notes that taxes are generally prorated between the parties and says nothing is paid to the Collector at the sale itself. Because the tax is a lien that stays with the property, a buyer inherits any unpaid amount. Parcels with unpaid tax can go to the annual tax certificate sale, held the fourth Monday of August at the Harrisonville courthouse.

If a bill still arrives in your name after you sell, give the Collector the new owner's name and address. Chris Molendorp is the Collector, at 2725 Cantrell Road in Harrisonville, 816-380-8377, and the Assessor is next door at 2733 Cantrell Road, 816-380-8400.

What should a Belton seller line up before listing?

A short checklist keeps surprises out of the contract period. Belton's own portals and the county offices hold most of what you need.

  • Rental registration and inspection results, if the house has been leased.
  • A look at the eTRAKiT portal for open code violations or permits on the address.
  • The Cass County tax statement and parcel number from the Collector or Assessor.
  • A copy of your deed from the Recorder, plus any release for a paid-off loan.
  • The school district for the address, since eastern Belton can fall in Raymore-Peculiar.

Belton's Old Town area hosts community events through the year, and the city's own planning documents describe it as a mixed-use district of small businesses beside homes. Route 58 and the I-49 and U.S. 71 corridor are the main roads through the area.

Where is the deed recorded after a Belton sale?

Deeds are filed with the Cass County Recorder of Deeds at 102 E. Wall Street in Harrisonville, phone 816-380-8118, open weekdays 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. The office cannot prepare documents for you, so use a title company or a real estate attorney.

The county also offers a fraud alert at casscounty.com/fraud that notifies you when something is recorded under your name. Under RSMo 442.400 an unrecorded deed binds only the parties and anyone with actual notice, so closing agents file right away. A Belton owner short on time because of repairs, tenants, an inherited house or back taxes may find a cash purchase shortens the schedule, with inspection, tax and recording steps unchanged.

More questions about Belton, MO

Does a Belton landlord have to register before selling?

Yes, every rental unit inside Belton must be registered, at $20 per unit a year. Inspections happen between tenants, so a vacated rental should pass before the next occupant or buyer moves in.

Is a short-term rental allowed at a Belton house?

Only with registration and a special use permit under Ordinance 2025-4950. The staff report puts the minimum startup cost at $270, and hosts owe the 5 percent hotel and motel tax.

What is the Cass County tax deadline for a Belton house?

Pay on receipt and by December 31. Late payment can bring penalties and fees as high as 25 percent in the first delinquent year.

Who handles the tax bill at a Belton closing?

Cass County says taxes are generally prorated between buyer and seller and no money goes to the Collector at the sale. The new owner pays the whole bill by December 31.

What is Belton's population?

The 2020 census counted 23,953 and the July 1, 2025 estimate is 26,193. Belton sits in northwestern Cass County within the Kansas City metro area.
